items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the penal law, in relation to establishing the crime of assault on the operator of a for-hire vehicle
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A10058

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the penal law, in relation to establish-
ing the crime of assault on the operator of a for-hire vehicle

PURPOSE  OR  GENERAL  IDEA  OF  BILL: To protect taxi drivers from being
assaulted on the job by increasing criminal penalties for such  assaults
to  those  currently  imposed  for  attacks on mass transit workers, and
posting warnings in taxi cabs about such penalties.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS: Section 1  titles  the  bill  the  "taxi
driver protection act."

Section 2 amends section 120,05 of the penal by adding a new subdivision
13  to define an attack on the operator of a taxi by an individual whose
intent is to cause physical injury as assault in the second degree.

Section 3 amends subdivision 1 of section 60.07  of  the  penal  law  by
adding  language  to distinguish indeterminate sentences from a determi-
nate sentence which shall not be less than three years greater than  the
minimum term of a determinate sentence, and paragraph b of subdivision 2
of  section  60.07 of the penal law to specify that a "for-hire vehicle"
shall mean a vehicle designed to carry not more  than  nine  passengers.
Also  a  new subdivision 3 is added to section 60.07 of the penal law to
require each for-hire vehicle to post a sign inside their vehicle  warn-
ing  that  "assaulting a taxi driver is felony punishable by up to seven
years in prison."

Section 4 provides for the act to take effect immediately.

JUSTIFICATION: According to an OSHA study from 2000,  taxi  workers  are
sixty times more likely to be killed on the job than other workers.  New
York City is home to the largest taxi driver industry in the country.

Defining  attacks on taxi drivers as a separate offense would underscore
the gravity of the crime. It would likely lead to more prosecutions  for
offenses  carrying enhanced sentences, as prosecutors would only need to
know that the elements of the crime were present, and not the details of
a complicated sentencing provision. And it  would  facilitate  a  public
information  campaign designed to inform the public that attacks on taxi
drivers are a very serious offense.

It would also bring consistency to the Penal Law by providing  the  same
treatment  for  crimes  against taxi drivers as for crimes against other
public transportation workers, and would bring New  York  in  line  with
California, District of Columbia, Illinois, and Pennsylvania, which also
make assaulting a taxi driver a distinct criminal offense.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: New Legislation.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:  None.

EFFECTIVE DATE: Immediately.
